edits.quote: Cover each shape with blue blocks in a different way on each copy. Draw around the blocks to show each way.
edits.fix: As written, the task cannot be finished. Each hexagon has one more copy than it has coverings: 3 copies of the small hexagon (2 ways), 4 copies of the 2-1-1 hexagon (3 ways) and 5 copies of the 3-1-1 hexagon on page 4 (4 ways). Change the task to 'Find as many different ways as you can. How many ways?' and add a box for each shape, or remove one copy of each shape.

edits.quote: Cover each shape with yellow, red, blue and green blocks. Use as few blocks as you can.
edits.fix: Change to 'You may use yellow, red, blue and green blocks.' As written it sounds as if every color must be used. The best covering of the 3-triangle uses only three reds (answers: 3, 6, 5).

Change to 'How many blocks?' and say to fill the box only for a yes. Two shapes, the big yellow hexagon and the big purple chevron, cannot be made, so a child does not know what to write in 'How many?' for those.
Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on every page instead of a separate right-aligned page number.

k-1.summary: A good K-1 set with real ideas at an entry level: possible and impossible blue coverings (including the 12-triangle trapezoid that cannot be covered), fewest greens, multiple coverings of small hexagons, fewest blocks (three reds beat the hexagon on the 3-triangle), big-from-small shapes with two honest 'no' cases, and a first-or-second blocking game whose answer differs between the hexagon and the strips. Every diagram checks out. The one real fix is P3: it asks for a different covering on every copy, but each shape has one more copy than it has coverings.

edits.quote: and they may not cover a black triangle
edits.fix: Delete this from the shared rules. Only P3 has black triangles, and P3 already says they are cut out.
Delete. 'Cover each triangle with purple chevrons and green triangles' already says this.

edits.quote: Then fill in the table on the next page to compare purple chevrons with blue rhombuses on the same triangles. [table: Greens with blue rhombuses / Greens with purple chevrons for 3, 4, 6 on each side]
edits.fix: Delete the sentence and the table. They are a directed record-and-compare step, and the blue side-6 entry has no board anywhere. Keep the closing question 'Could purple chevrons ever need fewer greens than blue rhombuses, on any board at all? Explain.' (Answers: chevrons 5, 4, 8 against blues 3, 4, 6.)
Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on every page.

grades-2-3.summary: A strong development of kernel 1. It runs from possible and impossible boards (the side-4 triangle has even area but cannot be covered) through fewest greens on triangles of side 3 to 7, with a proof, and hexagons with two triangles removed (a and c can be covered four ways each; b and d cannot). It then covers chevrons, which never beat blues, and two balanced hourglass boards that still need 2 and 4 greens, so the counting bound is not the whole story. It ends with an invent-a-board problem (minimum 7 triangles). All boards are actual size and correct. The only cuts are the redundant sentence and the comparison table in P5, plus a misplaced shared rule.

edits.quote: These half-size copies are for drawing only. Blocks do not fit on them.
edits.fix: Delete. P1 already says to build on page 1 and draw on the small copies.

edits.quote: Give your six ways of covering hexagon C the numbers 1 to 6.  (also P3: "Write the chain letters for each of your six ways" with slots Way 1 to Way 6)
edits.fix: Replace with 'Number your ways of covering hexagon C' and give unnumbered answer lines in P3. As written, the pages give away that C has exactly 6 coverings, which undercuts P1's 'explain how you know you have found every way'.

edits.quote: In any covering of a hexagon whose bottom edge is one small edge long, the rhombus sitting on the bottom edge lies flat, so its top edge is flat too. The rhombus sitting on that edge also lies flat, and so on up to the top edge of the hexagon. These rhombuses form a chain.
edits.fix: Rewrite as a short definition that leans on the picture. For example: 'In every covering, the rhombuses stacked from the bottom edge to the top edge form a chain (shaded). From the bottom up, write R or L for the way each one leans; the picture's chain is R L R R.' 'Lies flat' clashes with the rules' 'Blocks lie flat' (flat on the table). The paragraph also narrates the existence argument, which can be left to the child or the adult.

edits.quote: Hexagons D, E, F each on its own page; pages 5 and 6 half empty with no lines, explanation lines only under F
edits.fix: Add explanation lines under D and E (the request is 'Explain how you know each count is right'), or set D and E together on one page. The boards are correct: 10, 20 and 70 coverings.
Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on every page.

grades-4-5.summary: A rich, correct development of kernel 2. It finds all coverings of the 1-1-1, 1-1-2 and 1-2-2 hexagons (2, 3, 6), maps the flip graph of C (farthest pair 4 flips apart), and uses chains (ribbons) to count 10, 20 and 70. It has three verified flip puzzles of 2, 6 and 8 flips (8 is the full diameter), round trips with a parity question, and the 20 coverings of the side-2 hexagon as a capstone. Every printed start and finish covering was checked as a valid tiling. The main fixes are the wordy P3 chain paragraph, with its double meaning of 'lies flat', and the 'six ways' wording that gives away P1's count.

overall.strongest: The grades 2-3 sequence develops the up/down obstruction from concrete impossible boards to fewest-greens proofs, then to balanced boards where counting alone fails, with every board correct and at actual size.
overall.weakest: The grades 4-5 chain paragraph (P3) reads as a lecture with an ambiguous 'lies flat', and P2 and P3 give away the count of six that P1 asks children to justify.
